front.title: Policy Language Binding for OAuth 2.0 Authorization

abstract.t: AI agents exhibit dynamic, unpredictable behavior that cannot be fully described by traditional OAuth 2.0 scopes. This specification defines a behavioral authorization framework that binds behavioral constraint policies to OAuth 2.0 access tokens. It defines the authorization_policy authorization data type and the binding mechanism that carries behavioral constraint policies in access tokens via authorization_details, shifting the authorization model from static permission sets to runtime behavioral verification. This specification standardizes the binding mechanism between OAuth tokens and policies expressed in any policy language, not any specific policy language. This specification also defines a reverse-guided authorization mechanism allowing resource servers to return structured policy constraints in error responses, enabling agents to dynamically adapt their behavior and construct appropriate authorization requests.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: AI agents differ fundamentally from traditional OAuth clients in that their behavior space is dynamic and often unpredictable at authorization time. When a human delegates a task such as "help me find and buy a laptop" to an AI agent, the specific sequence of operations (product comparison, price checking, coupon search, cart management, payment, shipping selection) emerges at runtime based on available products, pricing, user preferences, and agent reasoning. Traditional OAuth 2.0 scopes, which grant broad access rights without behavioral context, cannot express the fine-grained constraints needed to govern such behavior: an overly broad scope grants unchecked power (violating least privilege), while an overly narrow scope causes frequent authorization failures that interrupt the agent's task execution.

This specification builds on OAuth 2.0 and Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) by introducing a behavioral authorization framework: a behavioral constraint policy (policy) is validated and bound to an access token by the Authorization Server. At runtime, the Resource Server, acting as a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), enforces the policy; a Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates each of the agent's behaviors against the approved policy. This shifts the authorization model from "what resources can the client access" to "within what behavioral boundaries can the client operate," enabling the agent to act freely within approved constraints while every individual behavior is verified at execution time.

The policy also serves as a formal expression of human intent: when a human delegates a task to an agent, the policy encodes the boundaries of that delegation in a machine-verifiable form. The agent retains behavioral autonomy: it decides what to do and when, but every action is constrained by the policy approved by the Authorization Server. This enables a balance between agent autonomy and human oversight that is not achievable with static scope-based authorization.
This specification enables:

ul.li: Authorization Servers to validate, bind, and register behavioral constraint policies in access tokens;
Resource Servers (PEP) to enforce the policy at runtime, with a Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluating each agent behavior using a policy engine appropriate for the declared policy language;
Resource Servers to guide agents toward appropriate authorization via structured error responses when behaviors exceed approved constraints.

section.t: The authorization_policy authorization data type can be used in conjunction with the delegation_chain claim (). When a delegation hop carries a structured policy, the behavioral constraint policy defines the fine-grained authorization constraints that were approved at that hop, complementing the delegation lineage and attestation provided by delegation_chain.

section.title: Language-Agnostic Binding
section.t: This specification standardizes the binding mechanism between OAuth tokens and policies expressed in any policy language, not any specific policy language. The binding defines how the Authorization Server validates and binds a policy to an access token, and how the Resource Server (PEP) retrieves and enforces it at runtime, with evaluation by a Policy Decision Point (PDP). The choice of policy language is an implementation decision: different deployments may use different languages through the same binding interface.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

section.title: RAR Integration
section.t: This specification defines the authorization_policy authorization data type for use with Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) . The behavioral constraint policy is carried within the authorization_details parameter as the primary mechanism.
Key aspects of the RAR integration:

ul.li: Authorization Data Type: The authorization_policy type is defined for use with the authorization_details parameter per RFC 9396. It contains the behavioral constraint policy, entry point, and optional context.
Token Response: Per RFC 9396 Section 7.1, the access token includes enriched authorization_details as the primary mechanism for carrying the behavioral constraint policy.

Complementary Use: RAR enables structured authorization requests with type-specific details, while the policy binding enables expressive declarative policy definitions. Implementations MAY combine authorization_policy with other RAR types.

section.t: Resource Servers MAY advertise supported authorization details types via the authorization_details_types_supported attribute in Protected Resource Metadata (), enabling clients to discover which authorization details types are accepted before constructing authorization_policy authorization requests. This discovery mechanism is particularly valuable in multi-tenant or federated environments where different resource servers may require different policy structures.

The authorization_details parameter provides one mechanism for carrying the policy in the authorization request; this specification standardizes the binding of the approved policy to the access token, not the specific input channel by which the policy reaches the Authorization Server.

dl.dd: A declarative language used to define authorization policies. Examples include Rego , Cedar , and ALFA. The choice of policy language is an implementation decision; this specification does not mandate a specific language.
A software component that evaluates policies written in a specific policy language against structured input data. For example, Open Policy Agent (OPA) evaluates Rego policies.

The entity that evaluates a policy against runtime input and renders an authorization decision (e.g., allow or deny). In this specification, the PDP role is realized by a policy engine appropriate for the declared policy language.
The entity that enforces the authorization decision rendered by the PDP — allowing, denying, or adapting the agent's request. In this specification, the Resource Server acts as the PEP.

The mechanism defined in this specification for binding policies to OAuth access tokens, regardless of the policy language used. The binding includes the RAR authorization data type, the policy reference claim, and the reverse-guided authorization error response format.
A framework defined in for expressing fine-grained authorization requirements through the authorization_details parameter.

An authorization data type for RAR that carries a behavioral constraint policy within the authorization_details parameter. The policy defines the behavioral boundaries within which the client (agent) is permitted to operate, enforced by the Resource Server (PEP) with evaluation by a Policy Decision Point (PDP) against each runtime behavior.

An identifier for a behavioral constraint policy that has been validated and registered by the Authorization Server, included in JWT access tokens via the policy_ref claim defined in this specification.

section.title: Policy Binding Authorization Data Type
section.t: This specification defines the authorization_policy authorization data type for use with Rich Authorization Requests (RAR).

section.title: authorization_policy
section.t: The authorization_policy authorization data type defines the structure of a behavioral constraint policy carried within authorization_details. When approved by the Authorization Server, the policy is bound to the access token and enforced by the Resource Server (PEP) at runtime, with evaluation by a Policy Decision Point (PDP). The policy language is identified by the policy.language field, enabling language-agnostic binding.

dl.dd: authorization_policy
Object
authorization_details (RFC 9396)

section.title: Structure
section.t: In addition to the common fields defined in RFC 9396 Section 2 (such as actions, locations, datatypes, and identifier), the authorization_policy authorization data type defines the following type-specific fields:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. An object containing the policy definition.
OPTIONAL. An object providing additional structured data for behavior verification at resource access time.

section.t: The common RAR fields and the policy serve different consumers at different stages of the authorization flow. The common fields (actions, locations) provide a declarative upper bound on the requested operations and resources, enabling the Authorization Server to approve or reject the request without parsing the policy. The policy defines the behavioral constraints that the PDP evaluates and the Resource Server (PEP) enforces against each agent behavior at runtime with contextual input. This layered design allows Authorization Server implementations to function without embedding a policy engine, while the Resource Server performs per-behavior verification using the full expressiveness of the policy.

The AS SHOULD verify that the policy does not exceed the scope declared in the common fields (, Step 5). The Resource Server, as the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), bears responsibility for ensuring the evaluated policy behavior is consistent with the approved authorization scope at runtime.
The policy object has the following fields:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. The policy language identifier. Values are registered in the IANA "Policy Language Types" registry (see ). This specification defines "rego" as the initial value. Future specifications MAY register additional language identifiers such as "cedar" or "alfa".

REQUIRED (if uri is not present). The policy as a string in the syntax of the language identified by language. The policy MUST be syntactically valid in the declared language. If both content and uri are present, content takes precedence and uri is ignored.
OPTIONAL. A URI reference to an externally hosted policy. If provided, the AS MAY fetch the policy from this location. The AS MUST apply SSRF protections when fetching from this URI (see ).

OPTIONAL. An identifier that selects the rule, function, or policy within the policy content to be evaluated as the authorization decision. The semantics, naming conventions, and default value of the entry point are defined by the corresponding language profile (see for Rego). When absent, the language profile's default entry point is used. The entry point MUST evaluate to a boolean value for authorization decisions. Languages that do not require a named entry point (e.g., those that evaluate a policy set as a whole) MAY ignore this field.

section.title: Policy Requirements
section.t: Policies used with this specification MUST adhere to the following requirements, which are language-agnostic:

ol.li: Entry Point: When the binding uses the entry_point field (or its language profile's default when the field is absent), the policy MUST define a rule or decision point matching that entry point identifier. For authorization decisions, this rule MUST evaluate to a boolean value.

Input Reference: The policy accesses data via the input object. The structure and content of the input object are determined by the evaluating party (AS or PDP) and MAY include token claims, API request parameters, resource attributes, and other contextual data as agreed between the client and the resource server.

section.t: Policies are strongly RECOMMENDED to ensure deny-by-default behavior. The mechanism for achieving this is language-specific; see for the Rego language profile. This recommendation is not listed as a mandatory requirement above because the mechanism for achieving default deny varies by language (e.g., default allow = false in Rego), and policies that omit it still evaluate correctly — they simply return undefined for unmatched inputs, which the Resource Server treats as deny per .

Language-specific requirements, including syntax version, package or namespace conventions, and safety restrictions, are defined in the corresponding language profile appendix. This specification defines the Rego language profile in .

section.title: policy_ref Claim
section.t: The policy_ref claim is an OPTIONAL shorthand mechanism for referencing a behavioral constraint policy in access tokens. When the AS uses Rich Authorization Requests (RAR), the enriched authorization_details array in the access token (per RFC 9396 Section 7.1) is the primary mechanism for carrying the behavioral constraint policy. The policy_ref claim MAY be used as a lightweight alternative when:

ul.li: The inline policy content would make the access token exceed practical size limits (see );
The Resource Server already has a cached copy of the policy and only needs an identifier to look it up;
The deployment uses opaque (non-JWT) access tokens where token introspection provides the policy content.

section.t: When policy_ref is used, the AS performs policy registration as described in .

dl.dd: policy_ref
String

section.title: Structure
section.t: The policy_ref claim value is a string containing the unique policy identifier assigned by the Authorization Server during policy registration.

artwork.name: policy_ref in a JWT access token

section.t: The Resource Server uses this identifier to look up the full policy content from a local cache or via token introspection ().

section.title: Policy Context
section.t: The context field within authorization_policy provides additional structured data that the client wishes to include at authorization request time. Typical context data includes:

ul.li: User identity: the principal on whose behalf the agent operates (e.g., user ID, organizational role);
Execution environment: runtime conditions such as source IP address, machine identifier, or network segment from which the request originates.

section.t: The input object used for policy evaluation is constructed by the Resource Server (PEP) and is not limited to the context field. When the RS constructs the input object, it SHOULD merge the context data under a context key within input (e.g., input.context) to avoid key collisions with other input categories.
The specific input structure is determined by bilateral agreement between the client and the resource server, typically documented in developer integration guides.

section.title: Protocol Flow
section.t: The following figure illustrates the end-to-end policy binding flow. The behavioral constraint policy carried in this flow may be written in any policy language — for example Rego , Cedar , or ALFA — using the same language-agnostic binding interface defined in this specification.

ol.li: Authorization Request: The authorization request includes authorization_details containing an authorization_policy object with the behavioral constraint policy (policy and optional context fields). This leverages RAR (RFC 9396) for structured authorization requests.
Policy Validation: AS validates that the policy is syntactically correct and safe to evaluate (see ).

Policy Approval: AS determines whether the proposed behavioral boundaries are appropriate for the specific client and resource owner, based on client registration metadata, organizational authorization policies, resource owner consent, and token binding context (see ). The AS does not perform full runtime policy evaluation (which occurs at the PDP on a per-behavior basis).

Token Binding: AS issues an access token with enriched authorization_details array per RFC 9396 Section 7.1, binding the approved behavioral constraint policy to the token. The AS MAY include additional metadata in the authorization_details object (e.g., server-assigned identifiers or normalized policy content) but MUST NOT alter the semantic meaning of the policy without client consent.
Behavior Execution: Client (agent) presents the token to the Resource Server when performing a behavior.
Policy Extraction: RS extracts the behavioral constraint policy from the enriched authorization_details in the access token.
Behavior Verification: The PDP evaluates the agent's current behavior (action, target resource, context) against the policy using a policy engine appropriate for the declared policy language.
Decision: The policy engine returns an allow/deny decision for the specific behavior.
Enforcement: RS enforces the per-behavior decision, allowing or denying the agent's action.
Response: RS returns the result to the client.

section.title: Reverse-Guided Authorization
section.t: Traditional OAuth error responses indicate authorization failure without providing guidance on how to obtain valid authorization. In behavioral authorization, this is particularly important: when an agent encounters behavioral drift (its next planned behavior falls outside the approved constraint policy), the agent needs structured guidance to recover autonomously. Resource servers can provide this guidance through structured error responses that enable agents to construct appropriate authorization requests with updated behavioral constraints.

section.title: Error Response Format
section.t: When an agent's request lacks sufficient authorization, the resource server returns an HTTP 403 Forbidden response with a WWW-Authenticate header containing the insufficient_authorization error code and a policy_profile parameter. This parameter provides machine-readable guidance on the required authorization conditions.

figure.name: Reverse-Guided Authorization Error Response
figure.artwork:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden Content-Type: application/json WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_authorization", policy_profile="eyJwcm9maWxlX3VyaSI6Imh0dHBzOi8vcmVzb3VyY2UuZXhhbXBsZS9..."
{ "error": "insufficient_authorization", "error_description": "Additional authorization required" }

section.t: Per RFC 6750 Section 3 and RFC 6749 Section 5.2, the error response includes both the WWW-Authenticate header with the insufficient_authorization error code and a JSON error body. The policy_profile parameter in the WWW-Authenticate header provides machine-readable guidance on the required authorization conditions.

The policy_profile parameter value is a base64url-encoded JSON object. Implementations SHOULD use base64url encoding without padding (no trailing = characters) per RFC 4648 Section 5 to avoid quoting issues in the WWW-Authenticate header. The decoded object has the following structure:

figure.name: Decoded policy_profile

section.title: Relationship to insufficient_scope
section.t: RFC 6750 defines the insufficient_scope error for cases where the access token lacks the scopes required by the resource server. The insufficient_authorization error defined in this specification addresses a broader condition: the token may include adequate scopes but lack the policy-based authorization structure (e.g., policy constraints or user confirmation) required by the resource server.

For example, consider an agent holding an access token with scope purchase that attempts to create a $500 purchase. The resource server requires a behavioral constraint policy that limits transaction amounts and requires user confirmation for purchases above $200. The scope is sufficient, but the token lacks the required policy binding. The insufficient_scope error cannot express this condition because the deficiency is structural (missing policy constraints and confirmation signal), not scope-based. The insufficient_authorization error with a policy_profile payload allows the resource server to convey both the missing policy constraints (e.g., max_amount: 200) and the need for user confirmation (confirmation_required: true) in a machine-parseable form that the agent can act on autonomously.

Resource servers SHOULD use insufficient_scope when the deficiency is purely scope-based and insufficient_authorization when the deficiency involves policy constraints that cannot be expressed as additional scopes.

section.title: Policy Profile Structure
section.t: The policy_profile object contains the following fields:

dl.dd: OPTIONAL. URI identifying the authorization profile for this resource. This URI is an opaque identifier that the agent MUST NOT dereference programmatically to derive authorization requirements. The resource server and intermediaries MAY use it as a cache key or audit reference. If the URI is resolvable, the retrieved document is intended for human consumption (e.g., developer documentation) and MUST NOT be parsed by the agent as part of the authorization flow.
OPTIONAL. Array of scope values that the access token MUST include.

OPTIONAL. Array of attribute names (e.g., agent_id, user_id) that MUST be present in the authorization context established by the access token. For JWT access tokens, these are claim names that MUST appear in the JWT. For opaque access tokens validated via introspection (), these are field names that MUST appear in the introspection response.

OPTIONAL. Object defining policy constraints that MUST be satisfied. Each key is a constraint name; the value is an object with the following descriptors: type (data type), description (human-readable explanation), enum (allowed values), and required (boolean, whether the constraint must be provided).

OPTIONAL. Boolean indicating whether explicit user authorization is required for the requested behavioral boundaries. If true, the agent MUST initiate an OAuth authorization flow to obtain the resource owner's explicit consent for the submitted behavioral constraint policy. This does not mean local user confirmation (e.g., a modal dialog) is sufficient; the authorization must be obtained through the AS to produce a token with appropriate grants. The specific interaction mechanism depends on the OAuth flow in use (e.g., the interaction_required error with JWT Grant Interaction Response , or the prompt parameter in the authorization code flow).

REQUIRED. Identifier of the authorization server capable of issuing tokens that satisfy these requirements. The agent can discover the token endpoint and other metadata via OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata () or OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata () using this identifier.

section.title: Agent Adaptive Behavior
section.t: Upon receiving a reverse-guided authorization response, the AI agent SHOULD:

ol.li: Parse the policy_profile to understand authorization requirements.
Verify that the specified auth_server is trusted before proceeding.

Construct a new authorization request including required scopes, a behavioral constraint policy that satisfies the constraints specified in the policy_profile, and any additional parameters required by the resource server.
If confirmation_required is true, initiate user consent flow.
Discover the token endpoint via the auth_server's metadata (RFC 8414) and submit the authorization request.

section.t: This adaptive approach enables agents to "learn" authorization requirements dynamically, reducing the need for pre-programmed knowledge of each resource server's policies.

During multi-step task execution, an agent may encounter behavioral drift: situations where the next behavior in its plan falls outside the approved policy constraints. When this occurs, the agent has three options: (1) request a new authorization with an updated policy that accommodates the new behavior (using the reverse-guided authorization mechanism described above); (2) degrade its behavior to stay within the approved constraints (e.g., selecting an alternative, less privileged action); or (3) request human confirmation to approve an expanded behavioral boundary. The choice among these options depends on the agent's task context and the confirmation_required signal from the resource server. Implementations SHOULD prefer degradation over re-authorization for minor boundary violations to avoid excessive authorization round-trips in long-running agent workflows.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: Security considerations specific to reverse-guided authorization, including auth server verification and constraint validation, are described in .

section.title: Policy Validation
section.t: Upon receiving an authorization_details request containing the authorization_policy type, the AS MUST perform the following validation steps:

ol.li: Language Check: Verify that the policy.language field contains a value registered in the IANA "Policy Language Types" registry (see ).
Syntax Check: Parse the policy and verify it is syntactically valid for the declared language. Language-specific validation rules are defined in the corresponding language profile (see for Rego).
Entry Point Check: Verify the policy defines the rule or decision point identified by the entry_point field, or by the language profile's default entry point when the field is absent.
Safety Check: Ensure the policy does not contain dangerous operations. The specific restrictions are language-specific; see for Rego-specific safety requirements.

Behavioral Boundary Check: Verify that the RAR common fields (actions, locations) do not exceed the client's registered permissions. This check provides an approximate upper-bound enforcement based on declarative fields rather than full policy AST analysis. The AS MAY perform lightweight static analysis of the policy (e.g., extracting referenced action values) to detect obvious inconsistencies between the policy content and the declared RAR fields.

section.title: Policy Registration
section.t: When the AS issues a policy_ref claim instead of embedding the full policy in authorization_details, the AS MUST register the policy:

ol.li: Assign a unique policy identifier;
Store the policy content;
Associate the policy with the authorization session;
Optionally, pre-compile the policy for faster evaluation.

section.t: When the AS embeds the validated policy directly in the enriched authorization_details (the primary path), explicit registration is not required; the policy travels with the token.

Policy registration in this specification is dynamic and on-demand. The Authorization Server does not need to maintain a pre-configured catalog of policies. When a behavioral constraint policy is submitted for binding, the AS evaluates it against pre-established approval principles (see ) and registers it only if approved. This eliminates the operational burden of pre-deploying policies for every anticipated agent behavior, which is impractical given the dynamic and unpredictable nature of AI agent workflows.

Deployments MAY also pre-register policies for well-known agent workflows (e.g., automated reconciliation, scheduled reporting) where the behavioral boundaries are stable and known in advance. In such cases, the agent can reference the pre-registered policy by identifier rather than submitting the full policy content in each authorization request. Both modes are supported: dynamic registration is the default for exploratory agent tasks, while pre-registration is an optimization for predictable workflows.

section.title: Error Responses
section.t: If policy validation or approval fails, the AS MUST return an error response per RFC 6749 Section 5.2. The following table consolidates the error taxonomy for policy-related conditions. The AS selects the error code based on the nature of the failure:

table.name: AS Error Taxonomy for Policy Binding

tr.td: URI fetching prohibited by AS policy
Language identifier not in IANA registry
Dangerous language features (e.g., http.send, ReDoS patterns)
RAR common fields exceed client's registered permissions
Other policy approval failures (e.g., organizational policy denies this pattern)

section.title: Policy Approval Basis
section.t: The Authorization Server's approval of a behavioral constraint policy is not limited to syntactic validation. The AS determines whether the proposed behavioral boundaries are appropriate for the specific client and resource owner based on the following factors:

ul.li: Client registration metadata: Pre-registered client capabilities, allowed scopes, and trust level established during OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration or out-of-band provisioning.
Organizational authorization policies: Administrative rules defining which behavioral patterns are permitted for specific client types, user roles, or resource classes within the deployment.

Resource owner consent: Explicit authorization from the resource owner approving the submitted behavioral boundaries, obtained through the OAuth 2.0 authorization interaction (e.g., the consent screen in the authorization code flow, or the interaction_uri mechanism in JWT Grant Interaction Response).
Token binding context: The authorization grant type, requested scopes, and other token request parameters that establish the context in which the behavioral constraint policy is evaluated.

section.t: For example, the AS MAY maintain a per-client allowlist of approved behavioral patterns (e.g., permitted actions, maximum transaction limits, allowed resource classes). When a new behavioral constraint policy is submitted, the AS verifies that the declared RAR common fields (actions, locations) fall within the client's pre-approved boundaries. If the proposed policy exceeds these boundaries, the AS SHOULD return invalid_scope when the behavioral boundaries exceed the client's registered permissions, or invalid_request for other policy violations (see the consolidated taxonomy in ). Alternatively, the AS MAY escalate to the resource owner for explicit consent before issuing the token.

This layered approval model ensures that the behavioral constraint policy carried in the access token is trusted not only for its syntactic correctness but also for its alignment with the authorization policies governing the client-resource owner relationship. The Resource Server can rely on this trust when enforcing the approved policy at runtime.

section.title: Refresh Token Handling
section.t: When an access token carrying a behavioral constraint policy expires and the client obtains a new access token via a refresh token, the AS re-binds the same approved policy to the new access token. The client does not resubmit the policy in the refresh request; the AS retrieves it from the authorization session state associated with the refresh token.

Refresh is a token-renewal operation, not an authorization request. A refresh request MUST NOT modify the approved behavioral constraint policy. If the agent's task requires different behavioral boundaries, the agent MUST either initiate a new authorization request (using the reverse-guided mechanism described in if applicable) or use Token Exchange () as described in . Both paths go through the full validation and approval process defined in this section.

The refresh token lifetime SHOULD NOT exceed the validity period of the associated behavioral constraint policy. If the policy has a natural expiration (e.g., a time-window constraint), the AS SHOULD align the refresh token lifetime accordingly.

section.title: Resource Server Enforcement
section.t: The Resource Server acts as the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) in the behavioral authorization framework. It retrieves the policy from the access token, invokes a Policy Decision Point (PDP) — typically a policy engine — to evaluate each agent behavior, and enforces the resulting decision (allow or deny).

section.title: Policy Retrieval
section.t: The RS obtains the policy from the access token. The primary mechanism is to extract the policy from the enriched authorization_details array included in the token per RFC 9396 Section 7.1.

The binding between the policy and the access token depends on the token type. For JWT access tokens, the policy content or policy_ref claim is integrity-protected by the token signature. For opaque tokens, the binding is established through token introspection or a shared back-channel between the AS and RS.
When the token uses the policy_ref claim instead of inline policy content, the RS retrieves the policy using one of the following methods:

ul.li: Local Cache: Use a cached copy if available and not expired.
Introspection: Retrieve the policy content via token introspection .

section.title: Policy Engine Integration
section.t: After extracting the policy from the token, the RS MUST load the policy into a policy engine compatible with the language declared in the policy.language field before querying it. The specific integration mechanism depends on the policy language and engine used. For language-specific integration patterns, see the corresponding language profile appendix (e.g., for Rego and OPA integration).
Once loaded, the RS queries the policy engine with the request context as input. The input structure is described in .

section.title: Enforcement Decision
section.t: Based on the policy engine's response:

ul.li: If result is true: Allow the agent's behavior;
If result is false: Deny the behavior with 403 Forbidden;

If result is undefined (the policy engine returns an empty object with no result field): Deny with 403 Forbidden. Policies that follow deny-by-default conventions (see ) will always produce a defined boolean result, so undefined only occurs when the default declaration is omitted;
If the policy engine is unreachable or encounters an internal error: Deny with 500 Internal Server Error.

section.title: Applicability to Different Authorization Flows
section.t: The authorization_policy authorization data type defined in this specification can be used with any OAuth 2.0 authorization flow that supports Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) . This section illustrates usage with flows that are particularly relevant to AI agent scenarios.

section.title: JWT Grant with Interaction Response
section.t:
The JWT Authorization Grant Interaction Response
is the RECOMMENDED flow for AI agent scenarios. In this flow, an agent presents a JWT assertion to the token endpoint. If user interaction (e.g., consent) is required before the token can be issued, the AS returns an interaction_required error with an interaction_uri where the user can complete the interaction. The agent then polls for the token.

When combined with policy binding, the agent includes authorization_details containing the authorization_policy type in the JWT grant request. The AS validates the behavioral constraint policy, performs behavioral boundary checks, and determines whether user consent is needed before issuing the token.

figure.name: JWT Grant Request with Policy Binding
figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Ajwt-bearer &assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9... &authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22authorization_policy%22%2C %22policy%22%3A%7B%22language%22%3A%22rego%22%2C %22content%22%3A%22package%20agent%5Cn... %22entry_point%22%3A%22allow%22%7D%2C %22actions%22%3A%5B%22search_products%22%2C%22add_to_cart%22%5D%7D%5D

section.t: After the user completes the interaction, the agent retries the same JWT grant request. The AS then issues the access token with the enriched authorization_details containing the validated policy.

section.title: Client Credentials Grant
section.t: In machine-to-machine scenarios using client credentials, the behavioral constraint policy can be included in the token request:

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=client_credentials &client_id=spiffe%3A%2F%2Fagent.example%2Fagent &client_assertion_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Aclient-assertion-type%3Ajwt-bearer &client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs... &authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22authorization_policy%22%2C %22policy%22%3A%7B%22language%22%3A%22rego%22%2C%22content%22%3A%22...%22%2C %22entry_point%22%3A%22allow%22%7D%7D%5D

section.title: Token Exchange (RFC 8693)
section.t: When exchanging tokens , a new behavioral constraint policy can be provided to refine or restrict the approved behavioral boundaries:

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Atoken-exchange &subject_token=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9... &subject_token_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Atoken-type%3Aaccess_token &authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22authorization_policy%22%2C %22policy%22%3A%7B%22language%22%3A%22rego%22%2C%22content%22%3A%22...%22%2C %22entry_point%22%3A%22allow%22%7D%7D%5D

section.t: The resulting access token MUST include the new behavioral constraint policy. The AS SHOULD verify that the new policy does not appear to grant permissions exceeding those of the original token. The AS MAY use the RAR common fields (actions, locations) as an approximation, since comparing two policies for semantic subset containment is undecidable in the general case.

Token Exchange is a common trigger for behavioral drift: when an agent's next planned behavior falls outside the approved policy constraints, the Resource Server can return an insufficient_authorization error with a policy_profile (as defined in ), guiding the agent toward constructing an appropriate Token Exchange request with an updated behavioral constraint policy. This enables multi-hop delegation scenarios where each hop progressively refines the behavioral boundaries to match the delegatee's specific task requirements.

section.title: Trust Model
section.t: The behavioral authorization framework defined in this specification relies on the following trust assumptions, which deployments MUST evaluate before adoption:

ul.li: AS-to-RS trust: The Resource Server trusts the Authorization Server to validate, approve, and bind behavioral constraint policies to access tokens. The RS enforces the policy approved by the AS and does not re-evaluate the AS's approval decision at runtime. This trust relationship is consistent with the OAuth 2.0 trust model in which the RS trusts the AS's issuance of access tokens.

Client-to-AS trust: The client (agent) trusts the AS to validate its submitted behavioral constraint policy and issue a token reflecting the approved behavioral boundaries. The client MUST NOT trust policies received from other parties (including resource servers) without AS approval.

AS/RS-to-client distrust: Neither the AS nor the RS trusts the client to act within its approved behavioral boundaries without verification. The AS performs static validation and approval; the RS performs per-behavior runtime evaluation.

section.t: A compromised or malicious AS could embed a wildly permissive policy in an access token, causing the RS to allow behaviors that the RS operator did not intend. To mitigate this risk, the RS MAY impose overlay constraints on top of the token-bound policy, such as:

ul.li: A hard deny list of dangerous or privileged actions that cannot be authorized by any token-bound policy;
Rate limiting or transaction caps that apply regardless of the approved policy;
Restriction of trusted ASes to a pre-registered allowlist, discoverable via Protected Resource Metadata ().

section.t: The choice of which ASes to trust is a deployment decision. Resource Servers SHOULD restrict the set of trusted Authorization Servers and reject tokens issued by untrusted ASes. The authorization_servers field in Protected Resource Metadata () provides a mechanism for the RS to advertise its trusted ASes to clients.

section.title: Policy Injection
section.t: Policies submitted by clients are evaluable policy definitions. Although policy languages used with this specification are declarative, they may support features such as recursive rules, regular expressions, and built-in functions that could lead to non-terminating or resource-intensive evaluations. Maliciously crafted policies can exploit language-specific features to cause denial of service at the Resource Server's policy engine. The AS and RS MUST:

ul.li: Validate policy syntax before registration;
Evaluate policies in sandboxed environments;
Limit policy evaluation time and resource usage;
Restrict dangerous language-specific features (e.g., external HTTP calls, unrestricted file access);
Restrict or sanitize regular expressions in policies to prevent catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS);
Enforce recursion depth limits and set size bounds.

section.t: Language-specific safety restrictions are defined in the corresponding language profile. For Rego-specific restrictions, see .

section.title: Policy Integrity
section.t: The policy_ref claim in access tokens MUST reference policies registered and stored securely by the AS. When the access token is opaque, the Resource Server retrieves the policy through token introspection (). The introspection response SHOULD include the behavioral constraint policy using the same mechanisms as the access token: either the enriched authorization_details array containing the authorization_policy object (the primary mechanism), or the policy_ref claim (the lightweight alternative). When a JWT access token is introspected, the introspection response SHOULD reflect the claims present in the JWT, including authorization_details and policy_ref, per RFC 7662 Section 2.2.

Resource Servers SHOULD invalidate cached policy content when the associated access token expires. If the AS revokes a registered policy before the token expires, the AS SHOULD also revoke the associated access token, causing subsequent introspection calls to return active: false per RFC 7662. Resource servers that observe active: false (or that are otherwise notified of policy revocation through a deployment-specific mechanism) MUST treat subsequent policy evaluations for the token as failed (deny-by-default).

section.title: Policy URI Fetching
section.t: When the uri field within the policy object is present, the AS fetches policy content from a client-provided URI. This introduces Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) risks. The AS MUST:

ul.li: Enforce HTTPS for all policy URIs;
Set strict timeouts and size limits on fetched content;
Validate that the fetched content is syntactically valid in the declared policy language before any evaluation.

section.title: Policy Size Limits
section.t: Policies embedded inline within authorization_details can significantly increase token request and access token size. Implementations MUST enforce limits on:

ul.li: Maximum policy source size (RECOMMENDED limit: 4 KB for inline policies). Note that JWT access tokens are typically carried in HTTP Authorization headers, where many proxies and load balancers enforce an 8 KB total header size limit;
Maximum policy complexity (e.g., nesting depth, number of rules);
Total authorization_details payload size in token requests.

section.t: For policies exceeding these limits, clients SHOULD use pre-registered policies referenced via policy_ref rather than inline policy content.

section.title: Reverse-Guided Authorization
section.t: Implementations of reverse-guided authorization () MUST consider the following security aspects:

ul.li: Auth Server Verification: Agents MUST verify that the auth_server specified in the policy_profile is trusted before submitting authorization requests. Verification SHOULD be performed by comparing the auth_server value against one of the following trust anchors: (1) the authorization_servers field in the Protected Resource Metadata () obtained from the resource server that returned the error; (2) a pre-registered allowlist of trusted authorization servers configured at client provisioning time; or (3) a deployment-specific trust registry. If none of these trust anchors are available, agents MUST NOT submit authorization requests to the specified auth_server. Agents MUST use only the token endpoint discovered from the auth_server's Authorization Server Metadata (). Blindly following redirects or trusting unverified auth_server values could lead to credential theft.

Constraint Validation: Agents SHOULD validate that constraint values are reasonable before including them in authorization requests. Malicious resource servers might attempt to induce agents to request excessive permissions.

section.t: All communications in the reverse-guided flow MUST use TLS to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks on error responses.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Implementations of this specification MUST consider the following privacy aspects per BCP 188 :

ul.li: Policy Content Privacy: Policies embedded in authorization_details may reference user attributes (e.g., input.user.tier, input.user.role). When policies are carried in JWT access tokens, these attribute references are visible to any party that can decode the token. Implementations SHOULD avoid embedding personally identifiable information (PII) directly in policy content and instead reference abstract attribute names that the Resource Server resolves at evaluation time.

Constraint Disclosure: The policy_profile returned in error responses reveals authorization policy constraints to the requesting client. While this disclosure is necessary for the reverse-guided authorization flow, resource servers SHOULD limit the information to what is strictly needed for the client to construct a valid authorization request, and MUST NOT include internal implementation details, database schemas, or infrastructure information.
Endpoint Exposure: The auth_server field in policy_profile reveals the Authorization Server's identifier. Deployments SHOULD use well-known identifiers rather than exposing internal service URLs.

Behavioral Profiling: The sequence of authorization_policy behavioral constraint policies submitted by a client may reveal the client's intent, capabilities, or decision-making patterns. Authorization Servers SHOULD treat behavioral constraint policies with the same confidentiality as other authorization request parameters and MUST NOT use them for purposes beyond authorization decision-making without explicit consent.

section.title: Policy Language Types Registry
section.t: This specification establishes a new IANA registry titled "Policy Language Types" for identifiers used in the policy.language field of the authorization_policy authorization data type. The registry is intended to be extensible; new policy language identifiers can be registered to enable interoperability across implementations that use different policy languages.
Registration requests MUST be sent to the oauth-ext-review@ietf.org mailing list for review and comment, using the "Specification Required" policy ().
The Designated Expert for this registry SHOULD verify that each registration request satisfies the following criteria before approval:

ol.li: The referenced specification defines a complete language profile that specifies policy syntax requirements, entry point semantics, safety restrictions, and policy engine integration patterns consistent with the structure and profile requirements defined in ;
The identifier does not conflict with or confusingly resemble existing registrations;
The change controller is clearly identified and reachable for future maintenance of the registration.

section.t: Future registrations MUST include:

Description of the policy language;
Reference to the specification defining the language profile;
Change controller.

section.title: Rego Language Profile
section.t: This appendix defines the Rego language profile for use with the authorization_policy authorization data type. Rego is the reference policy language used throughout this specification. When the policy.language field is set to "rego", the requirements in this appendix apply.

section.title: Rego Policy Requirements
section.t: Rego policies used with this specification MUST adhere to the following requirements:

ol.li: Package Declaration: The policy MUST include a package declaration. The recommended package name is "agent" or a domain-specific namespace.

Default Deny (best practice): Policies are recommended to include default allow = false to ensure deny-by-default behavior. This is not enforced by AS validation but is considered a security best practice for policy authors.

Rego Syntax Version: The policy syntax follows Rego v1 as defined in the OPA documentation . Implementations MUST use a policy engine that accepts Rego v1 syntax. Policy engines MAY additionally support Rego v0 syntax through backward compatibility mode to facilitate migration from existing v0 policy deployments.

Entry Point: For Rego policies, the entry_point field identifies the rule name within the policy package to be queried by the Policy Decision Point. When the entry_point field is absent, the default value is allow. For authorization decisions, the entry point SHOULD be allow. The corresponding rule MUST evaluate to a boolean value.

section.title: Rego Safety Restrictions
section.t: Although Rego is a declarative language, it supports recursive rules, regular expressions, and built-in functions that may lead to non-terminating or resource-intensive evaluations. Maliciously crafted policies can exploit catastrophic backtracking in regular expressions (e.g., regex.match("^(a+)+$", "aaa...!")) or trigger combinatorial explosion in set operations. The following Rego-specific restrictions apply:

ul.li: Restrict dangerous built-in functions (e.g., http.send);
Restrict or sanitize regular expressions in policies to prevent catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS);
Enforce recursion depth limits and set size bounds.

section.title: OPA Policy Engine Integration
section.t: When using Rego as the policy language, the Resource Server typically integrates with Open Policy Agent (OPA) as the policy engine. Common loading mechanisms include:

ul.li: OPA REST API: PUT /v1/policies/{id} to register the policy, then query the Data API;
OPA Go Library: Load the policy programmatically using the embedded OPA SDK;
OPA Compile API: Submit the policy and input together for ad-hoc evaluation.

section.t: Once loaded, the RS queries the policy engine with the request context as input. The following example shows the input object as constructed by the RS (not as submitted by the client). The RS merges the client-provided context from the authorization_policy object under the input.context key, and augments it with token-derived claims (e.g., user), request attributes (e.g., action, resource), and any other runtime data, as described in :

Note that when the OPA engine returns an empty object with no result field (undefined), the RS SHOULD deny with 403 Forbidden. Policies following the RECOMMENDED default allow = false pattern will always produce a defined boolean result.
